source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Provide a telephone number only and end the encounter without arranging ongoing support or follow-up.","B":"Require immediate separation from the partner even when the patient does not choose that plan and is not in immediate danger.","C":"Offer or refer to a multicomponent intervention with ongoing support while addressing safety and resources privately.","D":"Take no further action after a positive screen unless visible injury or immediate physical danger is present."}}
source_row.rationale: USPSTF finds benefit when women of reproductive age who screen positive for IPV are provided or referred to multicomponent interventions with ongoing support. Option C is correct and allows private safety/resource planning while respecting autonomy. A is too limited, B overrides patient choice, and D ignores a positive screen.
source_row.source_detail: 2025 recommendation: screen women of reproductive age, including pregnant and postpartum persons, for IPV and provide or refer those who screen positive to multicomponent interventions with ongoing support; a brief referral alone is not equivalent to the evidence-supported intervention. USPSTF Final Recommendation Statement dated 2025-06-24; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Health Promotion and Maintenance: preventive screening, immunization, pregnancy/reproductive health and age/risk-appropriate teaching activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: USPSTF — Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse: Screening
source_row.stem: A woman of reproductive age screens positive for intimate partner violence and is not in immediate danger. Which follow-up best reflects current USPSTF evidence?
